newsitem.title: USA: Colorado town reels after flash flood kills five.
newsitem.headline: Colorado town reels after flash flood kills five.

text.p: Residents of this college town Wednesday started cleaning up the debris left by a devastating flood that claimed the lives of five women.
Emergency workers determined that 40 people initially reported missing had all been accounted for, Colorado Gov. Roy Romer said.

"I'm informed that the death toll is five -- that all unaccounted persons have now been accounted for which really, really is good news," Romer told reporters at the site of a trailer park that suffered devastating damage.
All five who died were women. Four of them lived in two trailer parks whose homes provided little protection Monday night when a wall of water enveloped them.
City officials said 90 trailer homes were destroyed and more than 200 other homes sustained some damage. About 30 people were treated at local hospitals.
Residents were told they had to wait until Thursday before they could return to their mobile homes to see what they could salvage.

Romer, a Democrat, said $4.5 million in state funds will be added to a $500,000 disaster fund. "It will make a total of $5 million that will be available to begin to reconstruct and rehabilitate as of today," he said.
Romer said he also wrote to President Clinton seeking to have the area designated as a federal disaster area, which would make loans and grants available.
The weather cooperated with cleanup activities in Fort Collins, but flood watches were posted for rural areas in the northeastern corner of Colorado.
Several hundreds residents of Atwood were evacuated due to heavy rains that started Tuesday and left several feet of water standing, the Colorado State Patrol said.
The 35 families that live in Weldona were ordered to evacuate, Morgan County Commissioner Mark Arendt said, because of fears that runoff would contaminate drinking water.
Volunteers placed sandbags along the South Platte River near Sterling where 3.5 inches of rain fell since Sunday.

The massive thunderstorm that hit Fort Collins dumped as much as 8.4 inches of rain in the area during just 4 1/2 hours late Monday, turning the normally gentle Spring Creek into a roaring river that raged through the city.

Cars were overturned and mobile homes -- some gutted by fire from ruptured fuel lines -- floated in bloated creeks. Doors were knocked off hinges in buildings, while everything from kitchen appliances to toys were submerged.
Flood victims were hosing off articles, hoping to salvage at least some belongings.
Damage at Colorado State University, where deep pools of water stood only a month before autumn classes were to begin, was estimated at $40 million.
Computers and other items were lined up outside university buildings where workers sorted things that could be salvaged.

Most flash floods in Colorado occur in July and August and Monday's devastating flood brought back memories of a gigantic deluge 21 years ago that killed more than 140 people in the Big Thompson Canyon.
